title: Public X-inactivation data give no corrected evidence that LINE-1 repeats help Xist silence nearby genes; a published L1 link fails a spatial test, and L1 cannot be separated from base composition
abstract:
Public data do not give evidence, after correction for spatial clustering and multiple tests, that LINE-1 (L1) repeat DNA near a gene helps Xist RNA silence that gene. This matters because the Lyon repeat hypothesis, that L1 copies help X inactivation (XCI) spread, is a well-known proposed function of repeat (junk) DNA, and because the gene-level repeat-density test that supported it is common in genomics and can give false positives when genes and repeats cluster in large regions.

We re-analysed allele-specific RNA of mouse stem-cell clones with an inducible Xist transgene on the X or chromosome 12 (10 clones, 2,462 gene-clone pairs), RNA of human trisomy-21 stem cells with XIST on chromosome 21 (122 genes), and XCI calls for 483 human and 396 mouse X genes (genes that stay active escape XCI). For each test we rotated all sequence maps (repeats, GC, gene positions) together along the chromosome 1,000 times and compared the observed t statistic with the rotated ones.

On the mouse X, genes near more L1 were silenced more (+0.041 per SD; a Wilcoxon test as published gives p = 5e-5), but rotated maps gave similar values (p = 0.22). With composition of the non-L1 DNA in the model the L1 effect was +0.002 (95% interval -0.084 to +0.089), which includes zero and the raw effect. The human transgene data were uninformative. Human escape genes had fewer young (human-lineage) L1 copies within 100 kb (odds ratio 0.35 per SD, 0.15-0.80, p = 0.011) but not older L1, as earlier work suggested; an independent 2025 GTEx call set gave 0.61 (p = 0.34). In a cross-species test on 395 orthologs, human-lineage L1 did not predict human status significantly better than mouse-lineage L1 at the mouse gene (p = 0.20), and mouse escape followed human-lineage L1 at the human ortholog (OR 0.49, p = 0.011), against the Lyon prediction. No test passed correction (0 of 32 primary tests; lowest q = 0.26). Because XCI attracts new L1 insertions to the inactive X, the human pattern can also be a consequence of XCI.

Limits: escape calls are noisy and partly reuse earlier data; transgene silencing was measured after days; the rotation test has low power (about 25% at the published effect) and composition covariates can absorb a true L1 effect. We give lab tests, including an allelic test that holds composition fixed.

display.caption: Change in the silenced fraction of the Xist-bearing chromosome copy per SD of L1 (blue) or SINE (orange) density within 500 kb of the TSS, in four mouse data sets and one human data set. Left: unadjusted. Right: adjusted for distance to the transgene, expression and composition of the non-L1 DNA. Intervals: max(95% quantile of |t| over 1,000 joint rotations of all sequence maps, 1.96) x SE. The raw L1 association on the mouse X does not pass the rotation test (p = 0.22), and the adjusted L1 effect is not separable from zero or from the raw effect.

Odds ratio of XCI escape per SD of repeat density within 100 kb of the TSS (adjusted) for human (two call sets) and mouse (two call sets) X-linked genes, with rotation-based intervals. Young human-lineage L1 is lower near human escape genes in the 2015 consensus calls (OR 0.35, p = 0.011), not after correction for multiple tests; the independent 2025 GTEx calls and the mouse data are weaker.

Cross-species lineage test on human-mouse 1:1 orthologs. Left: young L1 near the human gene (human lineage) and near the mouse ortholog (mouse lineage) by XCI status. Right: joint logistic model (unadjusted); the Lyon hypothesis predicts that status follows its own lineage young L1 (blue below 1) and not the other lineage (orange at 1). No interval excludes 1 after rotation-based inflation.
